story:
Before he designed Central Park, Frederick Law Olmsted was a farmer on Staten Island, and the city says this black walnut is one of his. Olmsted lived in the house on this lot from 1848 to 1855, and NYC Parks, which named the walnut a Great Tree in 2024, credits him with planting it. The grounds hold many trees put in around 1850, and the walnut is the one Parks singled out.

That attribution rests on the Parks listing alone. No second source we have found names the planter, so read it as the city's account rather than a signed record. What anyone can check is the trunk, 52 inches across in the Parks measurement, or about 4.15 metres round. That is a serious girth for a tree on a suburban plot off Hylan Boulevard, but nobody has published a planting date for this one.

Olmsted left in 1855. Three years later he and Calvert Vaux won the competition for Central Park, and the rest of his career was spent planting on a scale this lawn never asked of him. The house survived and is now city parkland, with a second designated tree, a cedar of Lebanon, about 25 metres away.

In October the walnut drops round green-husked nuts that stain whatever they land on dark brown. If you know when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 4.15 metres round, the bigger of the two designated trees here. It stands east of the Olmsted-Beil House, about 25 metres from the cedar of Lebanon.

story:
The house behind this sycamore is where the American Revolution could have ended in 1776, and didn't. On 11 September that year the British admiral Lord Howe met Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and Edward Rutledge in the stone manor at the bottom of Staten Island and offered terms. The Americans would not take back the Declaration of Independence, the meeting lasted an afternoon, and the war ran for seven more years.

Whether the sycamore was standing then, nobody can say. It has no published age, and it would be easy to let the house lend the tree a birthday it has not earned. What it does have is size. When NYC Parks put it on the first Great Trees list in 1985, the trunk measured 65 inches across, about 5.2 metres round, and the crown stood 89 feet high with a spread of 55 feet. That makes it one of the bigger trees on Staten Island's list.

American sycamore is a native of river bottoms and wet ground, and its bark flakes away in plates to leave patches of cream and pale green on the upper limbs. Through winter the bare crown keeps its round seed balls dangling on long stalks.

The park around the house is free and open daily; the house museum charges a small fee in season. If you know how old the tree is, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 5.2 metres round, under a crown some 55 feet wide. It stands behind the Conference House, the old stone manor in Conference House Park.

story:
Japanese pagoda trees are planted on New York streets by the thousand, and almost none of them get this big. NYC Parks chose this one as a Great Tree in 2024 because it is unusually large for its species, with a trunk 48 inches across, about 3.8 metres round, at the southern end of Von Briesen Park where the path bends from north-south to east-west.

The park was once the private estate of Arthur von Briesen, a German-born lawyer who led the Legal Aid Society in its early decades and made it into the institution that still gives free legal help to New Yorkers who cannot pay. His heirs gave the grounds to the city in 1945. Parks believes the pagoda tree was part of his original estate, and that word, believed, is theirs. No planting record has been published, so the tree has no date, only a likely owner.

The species comes from China and Korea, despite the name, and it does its showing off late. In August, when almost everything else in a city park has finished flowering, it hangs out loose sprays of creamy white flowers, followed by bead-like pods that dangle into winter.

Von Briesen Park sits on the bluff above the Narrows, a short walk along the shore from Alice Austen's house and its London plane. If you know when this tree went in, tell us.

This is the last white pine of its size left in Blue Heron Park. NYC Parks says so in the 2024 listing that made it a Great Tree, chosen for its age, and puts its height at about 90 feet, as tall as a nine-storey building.

Eastern white pine is the tallest native conifer of the American northeast, and in colonial New England the biggest ones were so valuable that the Crown marked them with a broad arrow and reserved them as masts for the Royal Navy. Cutting one without permission was a crime. This one stands in a city park with a nature centre for a neighbour, and nobody is coming for it with an axe.

The trunk is 27 inches across, about 2.15 metres round, which is slender beside the oaks and elms elsewhere on the city's list. Pines grow tall before they grow wide. Parks gives no age in years, and nobody else has published one either, so if you know how long it has stood here, tell us.

story:
This street tree is a cross between a northern oak and a southern one, and Staten Island is where the two meet. Its parents are the black oak, at home across the northeast, and the willow oak, whose range runs up from the south and reaches its northern edge around New York. Where the two ranges overlap they occasionally hybridise, and the cross was first described from Tottenville, at the far end of this island, by the Staten Island naturalist William T. Davis.

NYC Parks made it a Great Tree in 2024, and its listing names it Quercus x filialis, the hybrid's botanical name. The common-name heading on the same page calls it a swamp white oak, which is a different species altogether. The Latin name and the story both point to the hybrid. Its trunk is 43 inches across, about 3.4 metres round.

The leaves are the giveaway if you know the parents. A willow oak has long, narrow, unlobed leaves; a black oak has broad ones with bristle-tipped lobes. A hybrid tends to land somewhere between the two, so look up and compare.

It stands on Stuyvesant Place by St. George Park, a few minutes uphill from the Staten Island Ferry terminal, which probably makes it the easiest Great Tree on the island to reach from Manhattan. Nobody has published its age. If you know it, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 3.4 metres round, on a sidewalk rather than in a park. It stands on Stuyvesant Place by St. George Park, a short walk from the ferry terminal.

Its silhouette on the hilltop of Sunset Park was the photograph Parks used to advertise the Great Tree Search, the public nomination drive that drew more than 270 submissions. In 2024 the elm itself joined the list.

The register usually works the other way round, with a tree becoming known because it was listed. This one was the picture first.

American elm is the species Dutch elm disease emptied out of American streets from the 1930s onward, and New York, with Central Park's elm walks, is one of the places where big ones still stand in numbers. The species grows into a tall vase, the trunk dividing low and the limbs arching out, which is exactly the shape that reads well against an open sky. This one's trunk is 38 inches across, about 3 metres round, modest beside some of the elms on the city's list. Its fame comes from where it stands. The central lawn of Sunset Park climbs to one of the higher points in Brooklyn, and from the top the view runs out across the harbour.

Nobody has published its age. If you know when it was planted, or remember it as a young tree, tell us.

Come on a clear day, when the silhouette is the one from the poster.

NYC Parks calls this elm one of many old-growth trees in Amersfort Park, which is not a phrase you expect for a small neighbourhood park in Flatlands. The elm is the one it singled out. Parks named it a Great Tree in 2024, described it as tall, and measured the trunk at 60 inches across, about 4.8 metres round. That puts it among the bigger American elms we list in New York.

The park's name is older than the street grid around it. Flatlands began as the Dutch settlement of Nieuw Amersfoort in the 1600s, named after the town in Utrecht, and the name lives on in this patch of green now that the farms are blocks of houses. Nothing ties this elm to that era, and the trunk alone cannot date it. Nobody has published its age.

American elm was the classic street and park tree of the northeast until Dutch elm disease swept through from the 1930s and killed most of them. A trunk this size in a Brooklyn park is something the disease usually did not leave behind.

One caution. The most recent public record we have of the tree is an observation from 2023. If you have seen it since, or know it has come down, tell us. And if you know how old it is, tell us that too.

story:
When this willow joined the city's Great Trees list in 2024, NYC Parks' description was mostly about where it sits. Benches and a path frame it, the listing says, which is about as honest a description of a tree's job in a city park as you will find. It stands near the Gerritsen ballfields in Marine Park, southeast of Ball Field 3, in the largest park in Brooklyn.

Weeping willows grow fast and are not known for long lives, so a trunk 38 inches across, about 3 metres round, is a big one for the species. The tree comes originally from northern China, travelled west along trade routes centuries ago, and became the standard waterside tree of European and American parks, with the long hanging shoots that give it its name. Here it is a ballfield tree instead, and it does the same work, a curtain of green over the benches in summer and a fall of bare shoots in winter.

There is no grand history attached. Nobody has published when it was planted, or when the benches went in around it. If you know either, tell us.

Marine Park has no subway station close by, so come by bus, and give yourself time to walk the park's salt marsh edges as well.

story:
The houses on this block of Albany Avenue are younger than the oak on their sidewalk. NYC Parks, which named it a Great Tree in 2024, says the tree predates the residential development around it, and believes it stands on ground that was once Paerdegat Woods, a stretch of East Flatbush woodland that the Brooklyn Paper reports was cut down in the 1940s.

If Parks is right, this is what the woods left behind. The woods went, the houses came, and this black oak stayed, a forest tree that has spent the decades since as a street tree. The trunk is 47 inches across, about 3.75 metres round.

It is not alone. About 240 metres east, at 1281 Troy Avenue, a second and larger black oak carries the same designation and the same story. Parks describes the two as probable remnants of the old woods, and a three-minute walk links them.

Nobody has put an age on either tree. A wood felled in the 1940s says when the trees around them went, not when these two came up. If you know how old they are, or remember the woods, tell us.

Both stand on public sidewalks in front of private homes. Look from the street.

The Brooklyn Paper reports that Paerdegat Woods was cut in the 1940s. The name is still on the map at Paerdegat Basin, an inlet of Jamaica Bay a few kilometres southeast, but on these blocks two black oaks may be the last standing pieces of the woods themselves.

Black oak is one of the native oaks of the New York region, a tree of dry, sandy ground. Its leaves have pointed, bristle-tipped lobes, glossy above, and the inner bark is a bright orange-yellow that once made it a source of dye.

There is no published age, and the date the woods were cut says nothing about when this tree came up. If you know more, tell us.

The fruit is green, fat and banana-shaped, with soft yellow flesh. The tree belongs to the custard-apple family, a mostly tropical clan, and has the leaves to prove it, large and drooping like a half-closed umbrella. In a collection laid out by plant family, it is the northern outlier of its own.

story:
This tree was a teenager in Brooklyn when the city declared it great. The United States National Arboretum in Washington sent it to Brooklyn Botanic Garden in 1971, and fourteen years later, in 1985, NYC Parks put it on the first Great Trees list.

It cannot have been size. The trunk is 12.25 inches across, under a metre round, and the tree stood 12 metres tall with a crown 25 feet wide at the time. What sets a Chinese parasol tree apart is everything else. The bark on young trunks and branches stays smooth and green, and the leaves are huge and lobed like a hand held up flat.

Firmiana simplex comes from southern China and is planted as a shade tree across East Asia, where it has a long place in poetry and painting. New York is toward the cold edge of where it is grown outdoors, and this one has now been here more than half a century.

The pin is approximate, inside a paid garden. Look south of the Rock Garden, about 25 metres from the mountain winterberry and a short walk from the Caucasian wingnut.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the smooth green bark of the young limbs and the huge hand-shaped leaves. It stands south of the Rock Garden, about 25 metres from the mountain winterberry.

story:
Mountain winterberry is usually described as a large shrub. NYC Parks measured this one at 27.5 inches across the trunk in 1985, about 2.2 metres round, with a height of 11.7 metres and a crown 28 feet wide. For a deciduous holly that is an outsized figure, big enough that it is worth seeing with your own eyes whether the trunk is one stem or several grown together. The register does not say.

The Parks entry links the species to the Garden's beginnings. When Brooklyn Botanic Garden was founded in 1910 it advertised a collection of 12,000 plants, and Ilex montana was among them. The entry stops there. It does not say this tree is one of the originals, and nothing we have found dates it, so read the 1910 connection as the species' history here rather than this trunk's.

Ilex montana grows wild in the Appalachian mountains, from New York south to Georgia, on rocky wooded slopes. It is a holly that drops its leaves, which surprises people who expect the glossy evergreen of Christmas cards. Female plants carry red berries into autumn; male plants carry none. Which this is, Parks does not record.

It stands on the south side of the Rock Garden, about 25 metres from the Chinese parasol tree. The pin is approximate and the Garden charges for entry. If you know its age, or whether it fruits, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a holly grown to tree size, about 11.7 metres tall, that drops its leaves in winter. It stands on the south side of the Rock Garden, about 25 metres from the Chinese parasol tree.

story:
People come to this corner of Prospect Park for the Camperdown elm, and the much bigger tree beside it is easy to walk past. The Japanese pagoda tree standing next to that famous weeping elm measured 86 feet tall in 1985, with a trunk 55 inches across, about 4.4 metres round, and a crown 62 feet wide. The elm is 6 metres high. Side by side, they are a lesson in what a tree can do when it is left to grow upright.

NYC Parks named the pagoda tree a Great Tree in 1985, and its note says the species comes from eastern Asia and was once planted at the graves of Japanese scholars. In Brooklyn it does its best work late in the year. In August, when nearly every other tree in the park has finished flowering, the crown fills with loose sprays of creamy white flowers, and the fallen petals pale the path beneath.

The tree has no published age. It stands in Olmsted and Vaux's park, but nothing we have found says when it was planted, and the park's opening date is not its birthday. If you know more, tell us.

This is a three-tree stop. The Camperdown elm is a few metres away, and the American hornbeam on the city's list stands just to the northwest, all of them a short walk south of the Boathouse.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the tall tree beside the low, weeping Camperdown elm, trunk about 4.4 metres round. It stands south of the Boathouse, a few metres from the elm.

story:
NYC Parks put this elm on its list partly as a lesson in shape. The English elm on Prospect Park's west drive grows from several trunks at once, and the city's 1985 Great Trees entry picks it out to show how the introduced English elm differs from the American elm, whose single trunk splits into the familiar vase. This one rose instead into a crown that measured 96 feet tall and 66 feet wide in 1985.

The combined measurement at the base is 74 inches across, about 5.9 metres round. That number describes a cluster, not a single stem, so it is not a fair comparison with a one-trunk giant like the Hangman's Elm in Washington Square, which is also an English elm. Stand under it and count the stems instead.

English elm is the species of several of New York's oldest street and park trees, and Dutch elm disease, which reached the city in the 1930s, attacks it as readily as the native kind. Fort Greene Park, a few kilometres north, has another listed English elm.

It stands between the Garfield entrance and the Meadowport Arch, on the stretch of the park closest to Park Slope. Nobody has published its age, and Olmsted and Vaux's opening of the park in the 1860s does not date a tree on its own. If you know when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its several trunks rising together, about 5.9 metres round as a cluster. It stands by the west drive between the Garfield entrance and Meadowport Arch.

story:
Dutch elm disease killed most of the American elms that once lined the streets of the northeast, and this one, at the corner of 72nd Street and Ridge Boulevard, escaped it. That is how NYC Parks put it when the elm joined the first Great Trees list in 1985, and it was the neighbours, not the city, who picked it out. Parks records that the community selected it for its remarkable size.

The size holds up. In 1985 the trunk measured 47 inches across, about 3.75 metres round, and the tree stood 78 feet tall on a residential corner of Bay Ridge.

The disease reached the United States around 1930, a fungus carried from tree to tree by bark beetles, and over the following decades it killed elms by the tens of millions. Whole avenues of them were cut down in American towns. Why this one was spared is not recorded. What the 1985 listing does record is that by then the people around this corner already thought it worth putting forward, and said so.

Nobody has published when it was planted. If you know, or remember the block before 1985, tell us.

Owl's Head Park is next door, on the high ground above the harbour, so the elm makes a good start to a longer walk.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 3.75 metres round, an elm of 78 feet on a street corner. It stands at 72nd Street and Ridge Boulevard, beside Owl's Head Park.

story:
A tree from the forests of northern Iran stands thirty feet from a public restroom in Queens, and it is there because of a nineteenth century nursery. NYC Parks lists this Persian ironwood as a Great Tree and ties it to Samuel B. Parsons, whose family nursery on this ground in Flushing imported and sold trees from around the world before part of the land became Kissena Park. Parks calls the species rare, and names this one as evidence of what the Parsons nursery brought in.

It was never going to be a giant. Parrotia is a slow, spreading tree, and in 1985 this one measured 16 inches across the trunk, about 1.3 metres round, with a height of 17 metres and a crown 44 feet wide. The Parks entry points to the bark, brown and flaking, a better way to know it than its size.

The season to come is autumn. Persian ironwood is grown in parks largely for this, the leaves turning yellow, orange and deep red, often all at once on the same branch.

Nobody has published when it was planted, and the nursery's dates do not settle it. If you know, tell us.

The Manchurian linden, another Parsons survivor, stands about 90 metres away near the tennis courts, which makes a two-tree stop.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the brown, flaking bark under a crown about 44 feet wide. It stands about thirty feet south of the public restroom in Kissena Park, 90 metres from the Manchurian linden.

story:
The man who photographed how the other half lived planted these two beeches for his wife's grave. Jacob Riis, the Danish-born reporter whose 1890 book How the Other Half Lives showed middle-class America the tenements of the Lower East Side, lost his wife Elizabeth in 1905. According to NYC Parks, he planted a pair of American beeches beside her grave in Maple Grove Cemetery that same year, which puts them at about 120 years old.

That planting story rests on the Parks note alone. No second source we have found confirms the date or the planter.

Parks listed the two as separate Great Trees in 1985, though they share one spot and one story. Back then one trunk measured 19 inches across, about 1.5 metres round, and the other 26.4 inches, about 2.1 metres. One stood 18.7 metres tall. Both have had four decades to grow since.

American beech is the native beech of the eastern woods, with bark that stays smooth and grey for life and leaves that often hang on, pale and papery, through the winter. Riis and his family lived in Richmond Hill, a short way from the cemetery.

The pin is approximate. Ask at the cemetery for the Riis grave, and check its visiting hours first.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as a pair of smooth grey-barked beeches, about 1.5 and 2.1 metres round in 1985, together at one grave. They stand beside the grave of Elizabeth Riis in Maple Grove Cemetery.
